title: Grace taken most widely includes nature itself
source_text: III. Porro cum non solum quae naturam superant gratuito nobis a Deo donentur, sed ipsa naturae bona, absque ullis nostris meritis, ex gratuita Dei benignitate habeamus, idcirco gratia latissime sumpta, ut Doctores iidem observant, naturae non opponitur, sed naturam ipsam comprehendit: quae quandoque gratiae nomine designatur, propterea quod est gratuitum quoddam Dei beneficium, gratis nobis a Deo collatum. Verum haec acceptio gratiae est quidem frequens in usu communi, in quo naturae dotes atque commoda gratiae divinae ascribere solemus, sed in scripturis & Scholis rarissima, & parum usitata est. Plerunque enim ibi gratia restringitur ad illa Dei beneficia quae naturae ordinem excedunt, neque ex natura fluunt, aut ad eam constituendam & conservandam necessaria sunt, sed ex gratuita Dei benignitate ipsi superaddita.
pass_a_gloss: III. Further since not only the things which surpass nature are given to us gratuitously by God, but the goods of nature themselves, without any merits of ours, we have from the gratuitous kindness of God, therefore grace taken most widely, as the same Doctors observe, is not opposed to nature, but comprehends nature itself: which sometimes is designated by the name of grace, because it is a certain gratuitous benefit of God, freely conferred on us by God. But this acceptation of grace is indeed frequent in common use, in which we are accustomed to ascribe the endowments and advantages of nature to divine grace, but in the scriptures and Schools most rare, and little used. For mostly there grace is restricted to those benefits of God which exceed the order of nature, and neither flow from nature, nor are necessary for constituting and conserving it, but by the gratuitous kindness of God are added over to it.
pass_b_english: Thesis III. God gives us freely not only what surpasses nature: the goods of nature themselves we also have from his free kindness, without any merit of ours. So grace in its widest sense, as the same doctors observe, is not set against nature but includes nature itself, which is sometimes called grace because it is a free benefit God has given us for nothing.
This sense is common enough in ordinary speech, where we credit the gifts and advantages of nature to God's grace. In Scripture and in the schools it is very rare and little used.

There grace is usually confined to those benefits of God that go beyond the order of nature: they do not flow from nature and are not needed to make it what it is or to preserve it, but are added to it by God's free kindness.
